In addition to nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA, it is conditionally recommended to include this as part of the evaluation process before initiating treatment for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. However, the quality of evidence supporting this recommendation is very low. 2. Screening for alcohol use and providing counseling to reduce moderate to high levels of alcohol consumption is strongly recommended for all individuals with HCV infection. This involves assessing alcohol intake and offering behavioral interventions to those with moderate-to-high alcohol consumption. The quality of evidence for this recommendation is moderate. 3. In resource-limited settings, it is suggested to use the aminotransferase/platelet ratio index (APRI) or FIB-4 tests to assess liver fibrosis, as these are less resource-intensive compared to other non-invasive methods like elastography or FibroTest. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 4. All adults and children with chronic HCV infection, including individuals who inject drugs, should be assessed for antiviral treatment. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 5. Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens are recommended for the treatment of individuals with hepatitis C infection, as they are preferred over regimens containing pegylated interferon and ribavirin. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 6. For patients with HCV genotype 3 infection with cirrhosis, and for those with genotypes 5 and 6 infections (with or without cirrhosis), an interferon-based regimen (sofosbuvir/pegylated interferon and ribavirin) remains an alternative treatment option. This recommendation was updated in 2016. 7. The use of regimens containing boceprevir or telaprevir is no longer recommended for the treatment of individuals with hepatitis C infection. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence, updated in 2016. 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for screening, care, and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis C infection were updated in April 2016. These guidelines provide detailed recommendations on preferred treatment regimens and durations based on HCV genotypes and the presence or absence of cirrhosis. 9. For individuals without cirrhosis, treatment regimens such as daclatasvir/sofosbuvir or ledipasvir/sofosbuvir are recommended for 12 weeks. For those with cirrhosis, treatment durations may extend to 24 weeks, and ribavirin may be added depending on the specific genotype and clinical scenario. 10. Testing strategies for hepatitis B (HBV) and HCV should consider the diagnostic accuracy, cost-effectiveness, and impact of different approaches. For HBV, testing for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) using rapid diagnostic tests (RDT) or enzyme immunoassays (EIA) is recommended. For HCV, anti-HCV testing followed by confirmatory testing for active infection using NAT or HCV core antigen is advised. 11. Dried blood spots (DBS) can be used as a sample collection method for serology or NAT testing for HBV and HCV. This approach is particularly useful in resource-limited settings, as it offers comparable diagnostic accuracy to venous blood samples. 12. Monitoring treatment response in individuals receiving antiviral therapy for HCV can be done using HCV core antigen testing or NAT for HCV RNA. These methods help confirm successful treatment response and viral clearance. 13. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is a significant global public health issue, with an estimated 250 million people chronically infected worldwide. The primary complications of CHB include cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), with 20-30% of chronically infected individuals developing these complications. 14. The risk of developing chronic HBV infection is highest when infection occurs perinatally (approximately 90%) and decreases with age. Universal HBV immunization programs targeting infants, particularly with a birth dose, have been highly effective in reducing HBV incidence and prevalence in endemic regions. 15. Despite the availability of effective vaccines and treatments, the majority of individuals with HBV or HCV remain undiagnosed and untreated. This is due to factors such as lack of awareness, limited access to testing, and competing healthcare priorities. 16. Screening strategies for HBV and HCV include population-based screening, healthcare facility-based screening, and targeted risk factor-based screening. These approaches aim to identify individuals at risk, link them to care, and provide appropriate prevention and treatment interventions. 17. Birth cohort screening for HCV, particularly in countries like the United States and Japan, has been implemented to identify individuals born during periods of high HCV prevalence. This approach has been effective in detecting undiagnosed cases. 18. The global burden of undiagnosed and untreated hepatitis B and C highlights the need for improved testing, linkage to care, and treatment strategies. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to reducing liver-related morbidity and mortality.
